transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, I... I guess I'm here because things have been getting really complicated at work, and it's mostly with how I'm communicating. I'm an artist, and I do a lot of commission work and gallery prep, so I have to write these artist statements and send out all these client notes. And usually, I'm really good at that, you know, I have my bachelor's degree in this, I know how to talk about my work and pitch my concepts. But lately, I don't know, it's like my brain is moving in ten different directions at once and it's all spilling out wrong. 

Like, I’ll be in a meeting, or I’ll be typing up an email to a client, and I'll start off talking about the physical textures of a piece—which makes sense, right, because texture is so important to the visual weight—but then in the exact same sentence I’m suddenly going off about the budgets and the financial constraints, and then somehow that connects to these... these secret meanings that are hidden in the materials, like how the numbers in the budget actually dictate the hidden message of the painting. And to me, it all links together perfectly, it feels completely connected, but people keep telling me they completely lose the thread. My clients are getting confused, and people in my meetings will just stop me and say they absolutely cannot follow what I’m trying to explain to them. It’s just so incredibly frustrating because I know exactly what I mean, I really do, but every time I open my mouth or sit down to write my artist statements, it just jumps from textures to budgets to these secret meanings, and I just can't seem to make anyone understand the connections I'm seeing.
Do you believe these connections and hidden meanings are definitely true, even when other people say they make no sense?

Well, yes, I mean... it’s not just that I believe them, it’s that they’re so obvious to me when they happen. Like, it’s not just in the budgets, it’s in everything around the work. For example, I’ll be looking at a canvas, right? And there will be this tiny, almost imperceptible stain on the gesso, or maybe a seam in the raw canvas that I stretched myself, and I just *know*—I feel it in my bones—that it’s not just a flaw. It’s a message. It’s like a specific instruction meant only for me, telling me exactly which direction the piece needs to go, or sometimes it’s a warning that I’m working with the wrong colors or the wrong client. 

And it happens with emails, too! I’ll get an email from a gallery director, and it looks like a standard update about an upcoming show, but I’ll read a specific phrase, like... like "we need to align our visions," and suddenly it’s not just corporate speak. It’s a direct, coded warning about my personal life or my artistic integrity. And it feels so incredibly real, so urgent. 

When I try to explain this to my studio mate—she’s great, she’s very grounded—she’ll sit down with me and say, "Look, it’s just a water stain from the leaky pipe upstairs," or "The gallery director sends that exact same email to all the artists, I saw it on her screen." And I hear her, I really do. I understand the logic she’s using, and part of me knows she’s trying to help. But even when she shows me the literal proof, the ordinary explanation, it is just so, so hard to let go of what I saw. The feeling of that hidden meaning just clings to me. It’s like trying to unsee a face in the clouds once you’ve already recognized it, you know? It just stays there, and I can't shake the feeling that the message was real, no matter what anyone else says.
During this time, have you been sleeping much less than usual without feeling tired?

Oh, sleep... yeah, actually, that’s been a whole other thing entirely. It’s funny you ask that, because I was just talking to my studio mate about this the other day. Normally, I'm someone who absolutely needs a solid eight hours, you know? If I don't get a full night's rest, I'm usually just a total zombie, dragging myself around the studio, making endless pots of coffee just to barely function. 

But lately... lately it’s been completely different. I’ll be working late, just really getting into the flow of a piece, mixing colors or working out those budget sheets I mentioned, and suddenly I'll look at the clock and it’s like 3 or 4 in the morning. And I’ll think, okay, I really should lie down, I have to at least try to rest. So I'll go to bed, but then... I only end up sleeping for maybe two or three hours. 

And the crazy part is, I’ll wake up feeling completely bright. Like, my eyes just snap open and I am entirely ready to keep going. I don't feel tired at all, not the way I normally would be after a night like that. It’s like my body just doesn't need the rest right now. I just pop out of bed and my brain is already running at full capacity, and I just dive right back into whatever I was doing the night before without even yawning. It’s actually been incredibly productive, even though I know it sounds a little extreme to people on the outside, but I just genuinely do not feel tired when I wake up. I just feel... illuminated, I guess, and ready to work.
Have you also been feeling unusually high, euphoric, or excessively irritable lately?

High... yeah, I think that's a good word for it. Or, I don't know, maybe 'lit up' is exactly how I’d describe it. Because for these long stretches lately, I just feel completely illuminated from the inside out. It's like I am almost unstoppable. I’ll be in the studio, surrounded by all these raw canvases and material samples, and every single idea that pops into my head just feels absolutely brilliant. Like, historically brilliant, you know? I’ll be mapping out a new series, and I can see the whole thing perfectly in my mind—the lighting, the spatial dynamics, how the audience will move through the gallery—and I just get this rushing, soaring sensation in my chest because I know it’s the best work I’ve ever done. It’s this incredible, vibrating energy, and I just feel so incredibly good and capable. 

But then... and this is the part that’s been really messing with my professional relationships... the flip side of that energy is really intense. If I’m in that zone, feeling so connected and brilliant, and then someone interrupts that flow or questions my process... I just lose it. Like, I have this collaborator right now, we’re supposed to be co-curating a small pop-up space next month, and the other day she made this tiny, honestly probably harmless comment about the color palette I was proposing for the promotional materials. She literally just asked if we could maybe tone down the neon accents so the text was easier to read. 

And I just... I snapped. I completely went off on her. I started going on and on about how she was diluting the vision and compromising the integrity of the entire show, and my voice got really loud, and I could see her physically backing away from me. And even while it was happening, a tiny part of my brain knew I was overreacting, but I just couldn't stop the anger. It felt so huge, just a total rush of rage that was so much bigger than the actual situation warranted. It’s like my skin is just too thin right now. One minute I'm on top of the world, making absolute masterpieces, and the next, just a small comment from a collaborator makes me explode like they just tried to destroy my entire life's work. So, yeah, it's this wild swing between feeling like an absolute genius and then just being so fiercely, overwhelmingly irritable if anyone gets in my way.
Have you ever had times when these hidden messages or special meanings were happening even when your mood felt completely normal?

Well... let me think. Actually, yes. Yes, there was. It’s so strange to think back on it, because you’d assume it all just happens at the exact same time, right? But there was this one stretch... it was a really quiet month, honestly. I remember it distinctly because I was finally sleeping normally again. I was going to bed at a reasonable hour, getting my full rest, and I didn't have that crazy, unstoppable, illuminated feeling at all. I was just... regular. Just me, showing up to the studio with my coffee, no vibrating energy, no snapping at anyone. 

But... the strange thing is, even with my mood feeling totally level and calm, those connections didn't go away. For several weeks during that quiet month, I was still completely wrapped up in it. I kept reading these intense, hidden warnings into the most ordinary studio materials. Like, I'd be sorting through my different grades of sandpaper or just looking at the way a bottle of linseed oil was sitting on the work desk, and the warning would just be glaring at me, telling me something terrible was going to happen with a gallery submission. 

And... well, I was also hearing things, too. I kept hearing these comments coming from right behind the heavy storage shelves in the back of the studio. You know those big industrial metal racks where we keep the oversized canvases and the extra framing wood? I would hear these distinct comments coming from right behind them. I'd put my brushes down, walk over, and look behind the racks, and of course, there was no one there, just dust and some folded-up drop cloths. But the comments would still happen, just sort of murmuring about what I was doing. So, yeah, for a few weeks there, even though my energy and my mood were completely baseline and I felt fine, the warnings in the supplies and the comments behind the shelves were just as real and present as ever.
Have you ever had a stretch of at least two weeks when the hallucinations or hidden messages were present even though your mood was not elevated or depressed at all?

Yeah, exactly, that's... well, that's exactly what I was just trying to explain about that quiet month. It was definitely longer than two weeks, for sure. Like I said, it was a solid month, maybe even a little longer, where my mood was just completely baseline. I wasn't depressed at all—no trouble getting out of bed, no feeling down or hopeless or anything like that—and I definitely wasn't in that unstoppable, illuminated phase either. I wasn't snapping at anyone or feeling like a historical genius. I was just... me. 

I was sleeping my regular eight hours, paying my bills, drinking my normal amount of coffee, just doing my regular routine. But even with my mood being completely, totally normal for that entire stretch, the other stuff just didn't stop. For several weeks straight, day in and day out, I was still reading those hidden warnings into the most ordinary studio materials, like the sandpaper and the linseed oil I mentioned. And the comments... I was still hearing those murmuring comments coming from behind the heavy storage shelves the entire time. 

So, yes, it wasn't just a day or two, it was weeks and weeks of dealing with the warnings and hearing those voices while otherwise feeling completely fine and level-headed. It’s just so bizarre to think about, because you’d really think they’d be tied to my energy levels, you know? You'd think if my brain was calm, the studio would be calm. But for that whole month, even though I was finally resting and feeling completely even, the messages and the comments were just as loud as ever.
Have these hidden meanings and voices been present continuously for at least six months?

Oh, wow, six months? It’s been... it’s been way longer than that, actually. I've been trying to piece together the exact timeline because, you know, when you're in the middle of a big creative project, time just sort of blurs together, right? Like, you measure time in gallery deadlines and supply runs rather than actual calendar months. But when I really sit down and look at when this all started... it’s been almost a year. Roughly eleven months, to be specific. 

I know this because it started right around the time I was doing the preliminary sketches for my winter showcase last year. I remember I had just ordered this huge bulk shipment of raw canvas and a new brand of gesso that I was really excited to try, because the texture is supposed to be incredible for holding heavy impasto layers. And that's when I first started noticing the messages in the materials. It was the way the canvas was rolled, the specific folds... they were telling me about the gallery submission. And then, not long after that, the voices started behind the storage shelves. 

Oh, and I didn't even mention the smells, did I? That started around the same time, too. I'd be working, and suddenly the whole studio would just reek of... I don't know, like burning plastic or ozone, even though I don't use anything that would smell like that. I even had the building manager come up and check the wiring because I was so convinced something was melting in the walls. But he couldn't smell a thing. So, yeah, between the messages in the supplies, the comments behind the shelves, and those weird burning smells... it's been going on for a solid eleven months now. It hasn't really stopped, whether I'm in that high, illuminated phase or just having a regular, quiet month. It's just become this constant, bizarre background noise to my entire life in the studio.
Have you ever had a period of at least one week where your mood was abnormally elevated or irritable and you had much more energy than usual?

Oh, yes. Yes, definitely. It's actually a huge part of... well, it's a huge part of how my creative process works sometimes, or at least how I experience it. There are these stretches, and they definitely last for a week, sometimes longer, where I just feel... lit up. That's the best way I can describe it. It's like someone turned the voltage up in my brain and I'm just completely illuminated from the inside out. 

During those times, I feel almost unstoppable. I'll be in the studio, and every single idea I have feels like pure brilliance. Like I'm tapping into something historical, something monumental. I have so much energy I feel like I could paint for three days straight without eating or sleeping, just vibrating with this incredible, productive force. It's amazing, honestly, feeling that connected to the work. 

But... there's a flip side to it, too. Because when I'm in that state, when I'm running on that high voltage, I can get incredibly irritable. Like, shockingly irritable. I'll be working with a collaborator, maybe someone helping me stretch a massive canvas or a gallery assistant talking about framing options, and they'll make just a small comment—something totally minor, maybe a suggestion about a different wire gauge or something—and I will just snap. I mean, completely lose my temper in a way that feels so much bigger than the situation warrants. It's like their tiny comment is this massive roadblock to my genius, and I just explode. And then later I think, wow, why did I yell at them over picture wire? But in the moment, when I have all that intense, elevated energy, it just feels like everyone is moving too slow and I'm the only one who sees the vision, you know? So, yes, those periods of being totally lit up and then snapping at people... that definitely happens.
During those week-plus periods when your mood was elevated or irritable, did your symptoms ever get so severe that you needed to be hospitalized or you were unable to function at work or at home?

Well, I've never been hospitalized for it, no. I've managed to avoid that, thank goodness. But... as far as being unable to function? I mean, I guess it depends on how you define functioning, right? Because I was still physically going to the studio, I was still physically moving paint around, so in my mind, I was working. But... if I'm being completely honest, and I guess I should be, the actual output, the professional side of things... that definitely fell apart. 

It’s hard to admit, but during those really intense, high-voltage weeks, I’ve actually missed some major paid deadlines. Which is a huge deal for me, because I pride myself on being professional. But I was just so caught up in the brilliance of what I was doing, the sheer magnitude of the ideas, that the actual calendar just ceased to matter. And it wasn't just the deadlines. I had these meetings with collaborators, people I really respect, and I would just... I would confuse them completely. I'd be talking a mile a minute, trying to explain these grand, sweeping concepts that made perfect sense to me, but they would just look at me like I was speaking a different language. 

And the worst part, the part that really stings, is that I actually had a whole exhibition postponed. My gallery rep had to push it back because the notes and the proposals I was sending over... they just stopped making enough sense to use. I thought I was writing these profound, manifesto-level descriptions of the work, but she told me it was just... fragmented. Like a puzzle missing half its pieces. So, even though I felt like I was doing the most important work of my life, the actual reality of my career was just sort of crumbling around me while I was in that state. So, yes, it definitely impacted my ability to actually function in my career, even if I didn't end up in a hospital.
Have you had any period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest or pleasure in things?

Depressed? Or losing interest? Um... no, I don't think so. I mean, I'm trying to think back over the last year, with everything going on—the gallery pushing back my show, the weird smells in the studio, the canvas folds talking to me... you'd think I'd get depressed about all that, right? Especially with the career stuff taking a hit. But honestly, no. I haven't really had any periods like that. 

Even when I'm not in that super high, illuminated state where I'm painting for three days straight, I don't crash into some dark hole where I can't get out of bed or where I hate painting. When the voltage kind of dial backs down, I just go back to my baseline, I guess. I still go to the studio every day. I still love mixing my paints and stretching my canvases. I still care about my art just as much. There's never been a stretch of time, definitely not two weeks, where I just felt completely flat or sad or like I didn't want to make art anymore. 

I know some artists talk about that, you know? Like the "tortured artist" thing where they have these massive depressive episodes and they can't even look at a brush for months. I have friends who go through that, where they just completely withdraw from the world and everything feels pointless. But that's just not me. My brain might get too loud, or the messages might get too intense, or I might get too revved up and snap at people, but I never lose that core drive or that joy in the work itself. So, yeah, no depression or losing interest for me. It's really just the extreme highs and then the weird background noise of the messages and the smells, but no real lows like you're describing.
When you’re in those high-energy periods, do you feel especially important or unusually powerful, like you have abilities or status that other people don’t recognize?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. It's... it's honestly hard to even put into words just how big that feeling is, but I'll try. When I'm in that state, when I'm just completely charged up and vibrating with that energy we talked about, I get this overwhelming, undeniable sense that I am doing something that is going to completely alter the landscape of contemporary art. Like, specifically installation art. 

I'll be looking at a space, or conceptualizing a piece, and I truly feel like I am on the verge of a breakthrough that no one else has ever even approached. It's like I have this profound, historical importance. I'll think to myself, "This is it. This is the piece that's going to change how everyone understands spatial relationships and materials." And the thing is, in those moments, it doesn't just feel like a hope or a dream, it feels like a concrete fact. Like I have this unique, unparalleled ability to see things that other artists are just blind to.

And because I feel so incredibly powerful and important, all the normal rules and limitations just seem totally irrelevant. Like, usually, an artist has to worry about funding, right? Or how much time it takes to fabricate something, or whether they have the technical experience to pull off a massive structural element. But when I'm running on that high voltage, I just brush all of that aside. I'll plan these sprawling, multi-room installations that would cost hundreds of thousands of dollars and require a team of engineers, and I just assume it will all magically happen because the vision is so pure and so necessary. I genuinely believe that those normal limits—money, time, physics, even—just don't apply to me when I'm in that zone. It's like my genius is a force of nature that will just bend reality to accommodate it. So, yes, I definitely get that feeling of being unusually powerful and having abilities that others just don't grasp. It's exhilarating, really, even if it leads to me proposing completely impossible projects to my gallery rep.
During those high-energy periods, have you been feeling much more sexually interested or sexually active than usual?

Sexually? Um... no, not really. I mean, I know some people get like that when they're all wound up, but for me, all that energy, all that intense, vibrating focus... it all just channels straight into the work. It’s like my libido just gets completely hijacked by the creative process. 

I actually remember this one time—and this perfectly illustrates it, I think—I was dating this guy, a musician, really sweet guy, and we were supposed to have this romantic weekend, right? But I was right in the middle of one of those high-voltage weeks, working on this massive piece with suspended wire and raw pigment. And he came over, brought wine, the whole nine yards, and he was clearly, you know, trying to set a mood. And I just... I couldn't even engage with him on that level. I was so consumed by the tension of the wire, the way the light was hitting the pigment dust in the air. I ended up talking at him for like three hours about the structural integrity of the installation and how the shadows were going to interact with the viewer's physical space. 

He eventually just left, and honestly, I barely noticed until the next morning because I was just so locked in. So, yeah, the physical intimacy side of things, the sexual drive... it just doesn't spike for me. If anything, it probably drops because I'm just so singularly obsessed with the art. The art becomes the only thing that matters, the only thing I have energy for. So, no, no increase in that department at all. It's all just paint and wire and space for me when I'm like that.
Have you ever had any hallucinations or hidden meanings when you were also in a clearly elevated or irritable mood, or do they also happen when your mood is not elevated or irritable?

Well, that's the really interesting part, because you'd think those things would only happen when my brain is running at a million miles an hour, right? When I'm in that high-voltage, world-changing mindset. But actually... no. They definitely happen when I'm totally calm, too. 

Like, there was this one period, just a really quiet month, where I was actually sleeping completely normally. I was getting a solid eight hours a night, waking up, making my tea... I wasn't feeling unstoppable at all. I wasn't vibrating with that crazy energy, and I wasn't planning any impossible, massive installations. I was just... baseline. Just going through the motions of a regular routine. But even then, for several weeks during that really calm stretch, the strange stuff just kept happening. 

I would be alone in the studio, and I kept hearing these comments coming from right behind the storage shelves. I have these heavy-duty metal racks where I keep my solvents and bulk gesso, and I would just be standing there, totally relaxed, cleaning a brush, and I'd hear these distinct voices whispering things from behind the metal. And it wasn't just the voices, either. I started reading all these intense, hidden warnings into my ordinary studio materials. Just regular things! Like, I'd look at a tube of cadmium red, or the specific way my palette knives were laid out on the worktable, and I would just *know* there was a message there. Like the manufacturer had specifically coded a warning to me in the barcode, or the way the linseed oil was separating from the pigment was a sign that I needed to be careful of who was coming into the building. 

It was so incredibly strange because, like I said, I wasn't elevated. I wasn't feeling like a genius. I was just a normal person trying to organize her workspace, and yet for weeks, those warnings and those voices behind the shelves were just a constant presence. I even tried reorganizing the racks, thinking maybe it was some weird acoustic echo from the building's pipes, you know? Because it just didn't make sense to me that my mind would be doing that when I wasn't in one of my intense phases. I spent days just moving boxes of canvas around, trying to find the source of the comments, but... yeah, they were just there, even when my mood was completely flat and normal.
Have the voices and hidden messages been present for most of the time since they first started, or do they only happen during mood episodes?

That is... wow, that's actually a really hard question to answer. I honestly don't know. It’s so hard to track, you know? Because... well, when you're an artist, especially doing the kind of large-scale, immersive installation work I do, your sense of time is already completely warped to begin with. 

I mean, I'll go into the studio on a Tuesday morning, and suddenly it's Thursday evening, and I've just been living on black coffee and the smell of industrial adhesive and raw canvas. So trying to step back and look at my life like a... like a timeline or a graph? It's just not how my brain operates. I've tried to think about it before, like, 'Okay, did the whispers behind the metal racks stop when I finished that big commission back in March?' But then I remember I was still checking the barcodes on my paint tubes in April... or wait, was it May? And in May I was feeling pretty baseline, I think, just doing administrative stuff and applying for grants. 

But then, on the other hand, sometimes I'll go weeks and I don't really notice anything strange at all. Or... maybe I do, and I'm just so hyper-focused on the texture of the materials or the lighting grid that I'm just tuning it out? It’s almost like background noise. You know how if you live right next to a train track, eventually you just stop hearing the train go by? It's a bit like that. I just haven't kept a diary of it or anything. My sketchbooks are completely full of structural diagrams and material lists and budgets, but I never really thought to write down, 'Heard the voices today, mood is neutral.' 

So, yeah, I really couldn't tell you if it's there most of the time, or if it comes and goes, or how exactly it lines up with my energy levels in the long run. It's all just kind of this big, messy blur of art and life and these weird, unsettling interruptions, if that makes sense.
Have you ever had a period when the voices or hidden messages were present while you were not having any mood episode at all, and for how long?

I know I kind of just rambled about this a second ago, but yes, exactly that. Like I was saying earlier, there was that one specific, much quieter month. The pressure was totally off, and I was actually sleeping more normally, which is honestly so rare for me. I was getting actual rest, waking up without that buzzing, electric feeling in my veins. I definitely wasn't feeling unstoppable or like I had to conquer the art world, and I wasn't depressed either. Just... neutral. Completely even-keeled. 

But even then, without any of the high-voltage energy or the mood swings, I still kept hearing those comments coming from right behind the storage shelves. And I was still reading all those hidden warnings into my ordinary studio materials, like the paint tubes and the palette knives. It’s so baffling, you know? Because you expect your brain to play tricks on you when you’re flying high and haven't slept in three days, but when you’re just... resting? It really throws you off balance. 

And as for how long it lasted, that specific stretch went on for several weeks. Just several weeks of me being completely fine, mood-wise, but still having to navigate these bizarre messages and whispers while I was just trying to sweep the floor or clean my brushes. I remember just standing there holding a jar of matte medium, thinking, 'Why is this happening now? I'm fine! I'm sleeping!' It's just exhausting, honestly, trying to make sense of it when you're supposed to be in a good, quiet phase.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when the voices or hidden messages were present even though you were not having a manic or depressed episode at all?

Yes, like... like I was just saying, right? I feel like we're kind of looping back here, but yes, absolutely. It was definitely longer than two weeks. 

That whole quieter month I was just telling you about, where I was finally sleeping like a normal human being and waking up without that... that intense, unstoppable drive to just conquer the world or build something massive. I wasn't high on that creative electricity, and I definitely wasn't in a dark place or feeling low either, because I was actually getting out of bed easily, making my tea, and just... being. Completely baseline. But even so, for several weeks during that exact same period, it was just non-stop with the comments coming from behind the metal storage shelves. 

It wasn't just a day or two of weirdness. It was week after week of standing in my studio, completely calm, feeling totally even, and still having to deal with those voices and still seeing all those hidden warnings coded into my ordinary studio materials. So, yes, definitely a period of at least two weeks. It’s just so vivid in my mind because of how incredibly frustrating it is to have your energy finally stabilize, to finally get a break from the emotional rollercoaster, and yet your brain is still... still finding secret, threatening messages in a regular tube of paint, you know? You'd think a calm mood would mean a quiet mind, but for those several weeks, it just didn't line up that way at all.
Have the voices or hidden messages ever continued for at least two weeks while you were not having any manic or depressed symptoms at all?

I... I mean, yes. Yes. I feel like I'm repeating myself, but yes, exactly that. Like I said, there was that whole month where things were just... quiet. Well, quiet in terms of my mood, anyway. 

I remember it so clearly because it's just so rare for me to have a stretch like that where I'm actually sleeping. Like, really sleeping, not just closing my eyes for an hour and then jolting awake because I have to go weld something. I was getting a solid eight hours, waking up feeling rested. I didn't have that buzzing, electric, unstoppable feeling where I think I'm going to revolutionize the art world by Tuesday. And I wasn't down in the dumps, either. I wasn't dragging myself across the floor or staring at a blank canvas and crying. I was just... fine. Neutral. Baseline. 

But even during that time, which went on for several weeks, mind you, it wasn't just a couple of days... for those several weeks, I was still dealing with the other stuff. I'd be in the studio, feeling totally even-keeled, maybe just sweeping up some sawdust or organizing my tools, and I'd still hear those comments coming from right behind the storage shelves. Just... whispering. And I'd still be looking at my ordinary materials—like, literally just a regular tube of cadmium red or a palette knife—and reading all these hidden, coded warnings into them. 

It’s just... it’s so frustrating, you know? Because you think, 'Okay, my mood is stable, I'm sleeping, I'm not manic, I'm not depressed, so everything should be fine.' But for those several weeks, it just wasn't. The mood was fine, but the messages and the voices were just... they were still right there with me, every single day. So, yes, to answer your question, absolutely. It went on for at least two weeks, maybe more, while I was completely symptom-free as far as my mood goes.
Outside of the high-energy periods, have these voices and hidden messages made it hard for you to keep up with work, relationships, or daily life?

Oh, absolutely. It’s... it’s been incredibly disruptive, honestly. Even when I’m not in one of those supercharged phases where I’m staying up for days, the impact is just... it’s heavy. It spills over into everything. 

Like, with my work, which is my livelihood, you know? I’ve actually missed paid deadlines because I get so caught up trying to decipher what my materials are trying to tell me. I’ll sit there staring at a canvas, completely paralyzed because the tube of paint seems to hold some warning I need to figure out before I can proceed. And then there are the meetings... I’ve had sit-downs with collaborators, other artists, gallery people, and I can just see the confusion on their faces. I’ll start explaining a concept, but my mind is so preoccupied with the whispers from the shelves or the hidden meanings in the room that my explanations just... they spiral. They stop making sense to anyone but me. 

It actually got so bad recently that an entire exhibition I was supposed to be part of had to be postponed. The curator was trying to work with me on the layout and the thematic notes, but my proposals were just... they were completely unusable. I was handing in pages of notes that I thought were brilliant and necessary, but to them, it was just disjointed nonsense. It’s devastating, really, because art is how I connect with the world, and when these... these messages and voices get in the way, it feels like I’m totally isolated. It affects my friendships, too, because people don’t know how to talk to me when I’m like that, but the professional side—losing work, confusing my peers, having shows pushed back—that’s where it really hits hard. So, yes, it definitely makes it hard to keep up with daily life, even when my mood is completely flat.
